Last year I bought a Jotter that sadly broke a week ago. When I ordered a new one, I assumed it would be the same, it wasn't. The pen was chunkier the engraving was nearly illegible, and worst of all, whoever placed the insert loosened the spring which stuck to the insert. I have no idea if this was just poor quality control or if this was just a new design. Regardless, I'm very unhappy with the pen.

I should say that I love Parker and the Jotter is one of my all time favorite pen designs. I have a lot of them and I have owned several of these pencils in the past. This pencil is a really good choice for an office pencil. What I mean by that is that it is very professional looking and goes well with the pen to be a respectable office set that looks good in a shirt pocket.
In the photos I have provided I am showing it next to the pen. The tip and plunger sections are different. The needle tip where the lead deploys is always there. The plunger/pusher on the pen is replaced with the metal eraser cap that you remove to get to the adjustable eraser. when it gets low you just pull the eraser up and continue to use it. You can get refills of the eraser.
The pen is very easy to load. When you remove the eraser piece, just by pulling it out, you have now opened up the section to load up with lead. This pencil is using .5mm lead.
Lastly, other than looking good, the pencil is sturdy. I have kicked these on tile, concrete, sat on it, dropped it, and overall there is going to be scratching and scuffing, but it has yet to break or the cap come flying off from where the pencil is. Luckily, I have not dropped it on the tip where the lead deploys, so that might damage it, but these stainless steel pens and pencils from Parker are pretty sturdy. So, it is good looking enough for the office and sturdy enough for every day carry.

So, you might ask why not a full 5 stars, well for a little bit less you get one of the best mechanical pencils on the market the Uniball Kuru Toga, that pencil rotates the lead as you use it to keep it sharp. With this pencil, like many, you have to keep rotating it yourself in hand to keep the line looking sharp and clean. Then for a little more, you get an excellent workshop pencil with great durability, excellent design, and useful for lots of more complicated pencil work in the Rotring 600 mechanical pencils. So, in essence I am docking a star because it does not offer anything interesting in a land of mechanical pencils that have some really cool features.

Things you may want to know:
Pencil, like the pen, is short in the hand.
Grip section is metal and narrow so it might not work for all grips or hand types
Clip is good looking and effective.
Not a heavy pencil, despite stainless steel. Very light.

It's a solidly constructed instrument. The ink cartridge appears to be brand new, and writes about as well as any ballpoint I've encountered thus far.

This is by no means the nicest pen I own, but it's a very nice knock-around everyday ballpoint pen. Great to put in the pocket or keep on hand when you need to jot something down, as the name suggests. I received it at the same time as a gunmetal Parker IM ballpoint, which is heavier and sturdier, and overall I prefer right off the bat.

This came with a working, apparently new cartridge. The IM came with a cartridge which won't write. It's disappointing, but these are refillable pens made to be reused, they aren't disposable. So bear in mind if you order a Parker ballpoint on Amazon, they have a reputation for coming with faulty refills. Consider a good refill a nice bonus, but buy it for the pen and just assume that you'll need to buy refills at the time of purchasing the pen itself and you'll probably be good.

As far as the working cartridge that came with my pens today, it writes as smoothly as any ballpoint I've tried. Much better than Cross. It's a ballpoint, so it doesn't look or feel as nice as a fountain pen, but for everyday use without having to worry about the considerations that come with liquid inks, this is a nice option. I'd consider getting another Jotter in a different finish for sure.

t: It is nice.  Not THAT nice, maybe.
x:
This is a decent mechanical pencil. The mechanism that feeds the lead works well. The provided lead writes well and doesn't break off under reasonable writing pressure. The pencil has good weight to it so it feels comfortable in my hand. I like to hold the pencil so the clip faces away from me and rests against my hand. This keeps the pencil a little more stable so that the point on my lead wears consistently. I worry about that only for my penmanship, which isn't great, but it is markedly worse when I don't keep track of the point on my pencil lead (it is different with the fine point of a mechanical pencil than it is with, say, a #2). Wow that reads like I'm a crazy person! Maybe I am. Or maybe I'm just someone who writes a lot and has learned what works best for me. Maybe it is a combination of the two.

The gift box is nice and all, but I think this may be tricky as a gift. I would risk putting the recipient in a position to appear ungrateful, which they may not be. Imagine opening a gift box and seeing this item. And you may even know the Parker name and logo by reputation. And whether you know Parker or not, I feel that most people open the box and see a pen and it isn't until a moment has passed that you learn it is a pencil. I don't know why gifting a pen seems more common, or even like a fun gift for the right person, but gifting a pencil seems less so. It seems to me that Parker wants to maintain its brand image and to put this pencil on a card that would hang on a peg is something they weren't willing to do. However, this is that type of pencil. In fact, my favorite pencil (which is mechanical) is that type of pencil.

t: Well made, elegant design - but not for me
x:
I have fairly large hands and I find this model of Parker pen too narrow and too short to write comfortably with.

It also feels slightly top-heavy: After shifting my fingers back towards the top to counteract the unbalance, the pen barrel feels too short, as if I'm writing with a 'stub'.

I think a pen with these dimensions would be best for people with smaller hands than mine.

According to the description this is a medium-point ballpoint. However to my eye the line appears closer to a fine ballpoint width.

As a positive, the retractor button is firm and the action feels solid, which I like. The writing tip is smooth and delivers an exceptionally even line at a pressure less than I normally write with - again people who prefer a light pen, and a light touch to their writing, will probably enjoy this model.

Bottom Line: A attractive, slim design pen that's sensistive to the touch - it just doesn't feel like it's made for my hand and writing style.

I bought this pen to replace a previous jotter than I had misplaced, and immediately thought that its quality was significantly lesser than the one I was replacing. Incidentally, I found the lost pen just yesterday, and after conducting a side by side comparison I was able to more accurately identify my issues with it:

The pen casing is pretty light, and I would rather it had just a little more weight to it. Feels kind of toy-like in my hand. Also the pen rattles when moved quickly or flicked, seemingly from the ink cartridge not fitting snuggly within the shaft.

The pen writes well enough, and it seems decently durable, but when compared side-by-side to my other Jotter I feel disappointed. It might be worth noting that this pen has "HE" engraved on the shaft where my nicer one has "Y". Also the nicer one has the gold clip, instead of the chrome finish.

All in all, it works as expected, but for the money spent I had anticipated a better quality product.

Overall this feels like a quality mechanical pencil. Here’s my thoughts:

• Overall quality looks good. Parts go and stay together nicely.
• Eraser is hidden under a top metal cap. The cap stays on very nicely and allows quick and easy access to the eraser when needed.
• Pressing the cap to release more lead does not work very well at all. It takes multiple clicks to get even a little lead out, and once out writing forces the lead back up. I’m not happy about this at all.
• The pencil feels a bit small for a medium sized adult hand.

Bottom line, although I’ll be using this device from time to time it will not be my go-to pencil for sure. This is a good looking budget mechanical pencil at most.

t: Nice Pen With A Couple Flaws
x:
I’ll start off with the pros of this pen. First, the stainless steel finish looks really nice. Second, the pen is surprisingly lightweight for being all metal. Third, it is very easy to hold, and isn’t top heavy. Overall, I’m pretty happy with the pen. I have a Space Pen that I absolutely love, and thought this would be pretty comparable. I think the Space Pen is better, IMO.
Ok, the cons, the thing feels a little cheap. It rattles when you shake it (granted, my Space Pen did too, but some well placed scotch tape on the ink cartridge fixed that). I tried using the same scotch tape trick, and it worked a little bit...there is still some spring rattle toward the business end of the pen. Also, the clicking mechanism doesn’t seem very sturdy, and has a hollow unsatisfying sound when engaging the cartridge to be able to write. If Parker tightened up the spring and the mechanism on the end of the pen, it would be a great pen, but with that, I could only give it 4 stars. Is it something you could live with, probably. But, if you’re looking for a sturdier more professional pen, you may want to look at a Space Pen instead, or check out other models/brands.

Fourth, when I opened up the pen to check to ink, the label was a bit washed off. This might be because it's a counterfeit ink or a used ink.
Lastly as someone mentioned on another review, it does smell a bit weird. Like when you receive a product from China and it smells? That kinda smell.

Rarely do I get the opportunity to use a mechanical pencil anymore. Most of my note taking is done with a quick-write pen, and reports are typed.

That being said, lately I have been doing some extensive hand drawn designs and schematics. This is where this pencil shines. It is my go to for all written or drawn things, that have potential for change.

It is fairly simple in it's function. It works just as well as a good mechanical pencil, like you'd expect. It doesn't have any fancy features like lead turning or custom barrels, tips, etc.

The build quality is interesting. It is listed as being stainless steel, but it is so incredibly light weight, I thought it was aluminum.

Aesthetically, it's an excellent choice. Perfect pocket height for those that like to store writing utensils in their shirt pocket for quick access. It also sits on top of the ear quite nicely, as I stated before, it being extremely light weight.

The grip is fairly ergonomic. There are no ridges, it nice and cylindrical with a small increase in diameter from the tip to the grip.

I will be using this pencil quite often.

Pros: Overall nice pen, lightweight (great for shirt pocket), easy to hold, writes well with equipped ink (blue Parker Quinkflow Medium). Excellent clickability. Very reasonable price. Stamped "Parker FRANCE." Don't have to worry too much about losing it. Unscrewing and screwing barrel pieces feels solid and well machined.

Cons: Not as heavy as I imagined the venerable Parker Jotter would be.

Neutral: Barrels do not quite line up, but if you're expecting them to hand-grind or hand-polish these barrels down to exact fit, then your mind is NOT in the right price range. I'm not a huge fan of the Parker "arrow clip," and a rubber O-ring might have been nice, but again, not really relevant to this price range.

It looks like this pen sells for around $25. While it is a nice pen, in that it feels good in the hand when writing and writes well, it seems overpriced at that price. It is quite lightweight and looks a little cheap to me. The gift box is a nice touch, but is nothing fancy and in fact has a plastic container that holds the pen in so securely you have to pry it out.

On the other hand, it does look like this pen will last a long while, and it seems to be made with typical Parker pen quality, which I have always found to be excellent. I was a little surprised to find it writes in blue, when I was expecting black.The ink cartridge is easily replaced, but costs about $3 for a single refill.

t: Best quality and most durable pen ever made!
x: This classic Parker pen has been around for several decades maybe back to the 50s. It is so popular they are even refill adapters for the pressurized ball points the astronauts used on space flights in the early years.  They are currently made by Fisher pens. Pressurized and write on most materials and in any position. There's absolutely nothing wrong with the Parker refills just as they come from Parker! This is such a classic pen that you see it in hundreds of movies, if you just watch for it. It's being used and in the pockets of a multitude of silver screen stars. I have never had one fail to click. Additionally, it fits deep in the pocket not sticking out where it can be grabbed by something you rub against and rip your pocket. My favorite pen!

t: Each year these get worse and worse
x:
Wow, what a disappointment. These pens are terrible and it's embarrassing they come in a gift box. I wouldn't be caught dead giving one of these to anyone I actually respect.

These days the Parker pen metal is super thin. The stamping is shallow. The mechanism inside feels cheap. This is a 99-cent pen at best. Maybe a buck fifty.

Each time I buy one, it arrives and I think "Wow, Parker pens have gotten EVEN WORSE than the last time I bought one." And then I vow never to buy one again. And then I forget how awful they are and end up buying one and the cycle continues. And, each time, they are indeed a worse product.

Parker must be cashing out for its shareholders or something because a company can't last forever spewing out bottom-quality junk like these pens have become. 10 more years and the company will hopefully be mercifully gone.

It makes you want to draw detailed lines and writing feels like the flow of a pen. Very light weight and has a controlled push for feeding the lead so you shouldn’t have to worry about lead wasted. I very much recommend buying this pencil. Only future problem is if I want to use an eraser, I will need to find replacements and purchase those to use since this product does not include spares.

A very simple yet elegant design. It has a somewhat narrow barrel, and is very lightweight, yet feels incredibly sturdy.  The 'click' action is very solid, as is the clip. It comes with a medium blue ink cartridge, which I initially thought I would have to replace with a fine point (I prefer very fine point pens), but I don't think I'll have to, as it writes very smoothly, even with a light touch (thanks to both the ballpoint and the oil-based ink), and very faithfully transmits my motions, even slight ones, into smudge-less and accurate writing.  I'm a fan.

t: Classy and sleek feel and look

The pen does not always fully retract when clicked and sticks out to varying degrees each time, ensuring that you'll accidentally get ink all over everything. It's very lightweight and flimsy feeling. I finally tried to stretch out the spring in hopes that it'd function better, but to no avail.

I'm amazed that by merely dropping the pen onto the floor, the "click" mechanism, which advances or retracts the ink cartridge in the barrel, would break!

Not surprising, though, considering this "stainless" Jotter felt much flimsier to those purchased in the past, which had much more heft.

They really don't make them like they used to, sadly.

t: I began using mechanical pencils in 1965 and enjoy the convenience
x: I like having a mechanical pencil to jot down notes whenever I want.  This pencil has a nice eraser and storage for replacement leads when the tip is used up.  It is a bit challenging reloading the lead, but I enjoy the feel of the pencil when I am taking notes.  Wooden pencils are fine but when the points break sometimes I am unable to sharpen them.  This is not a problem with a mechanical pencil and I always have a nice thin line to write with.
